questions.text: Let x and Y be finite sets and f:x[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Y be a function. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1 fails when f(A) and f(B) overlap.
- Option 2 fails for non-injective f: A = {1}, B = {2}, f(1) = f(2) = y gives [latex]f(A\cap B)=\emptyset[/latex] but [latex]f(A)\cap f(B)=\{y\}[/latex].
- Option 3 fails for the same example.
- Option 4: [latex]x\in f^{-1}(S\cap T)\iff f(x)\in S[/latex] and [latex]f(x)\in T\iff x\in f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] always true.

Answer: [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

For any subsets A and B of x, f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B) =f(A)[latex]\cap[/latex]f(B)
For any subsets A and B of x, |f(A[latex]\cap[/latex]B)| = min{|f (A)| ,|f(B)|}
For any subsets S and T of Y, [latex]f^{-1}(S\cap T)=f^{-1}(S)\cap f^{-1}(T)[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider the following statements:
P: Good mobile phones are not cheap
Q: Cheap mobile phones are not good

L: P implies Q
M: Q implies P
N: P is equivalent to Q
Which one of the following about L, M, and N is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Let G = good, C = cheap.
- P: [latex]G\rightarrow\neg C[/latex]
- Q: [latex]C\rightarrow\neg G[/latex]

Q is the contrapositive of P, so P [latex]\equiv[/latex] Q. Hence P implies Q, Q implies P, and P is equivalent to Q.

Answer: L, M and N are TRUE

options: L, M and N are TRUE.

questions.text: Which one of the following Boolean expressions is NOT a tautology?
questions.solution:
Check option 2 with a = 0, b = 0, c = 0:
[latex]a\rightarrow c=1[/latex], but [latex]\sim b\rightarrow(a\wedge c)=1\rightarrow0=0[/latex]. The whole is [latex]1\rightarrow0=0[/latex], so it is not a tautology.

Options 1 (transitivity), 3 and 4 are always true.

Answer: [latex](a\rightarrow c)\rightarrow(\sim b\rightarrow(a\wedge c))[/latex]

questions.text: A cycle on n vertices is isomorphic to its complement. The value of n is _____.
questions.solution:
A cycle [latex]C_n[/latex] has n edges, its complement has [latex]\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-n[/latex] edges. Isomorphic graphs have equal edge counts:
[latex]n=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-n\Rightarrow n=5[/latex]

Indeed the complement of [latex]C_5[/latex] (the pentagram) is again a 5-cycle.

Answer: 5

questions.text:
Consider the following relation on subsets of the set S of integers between 1 and 2014. For two distinct subsets U and V of S we say U[latex]\lt[/latex]V if the minimum element in the symmetric difference of the two sets is in U.
Consider the following two statements:
S1: There is a subset of S that is larger than every other subset.
S2: There is a subset of S that is smaller than every other subset.
Which one of the following is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
U [latex]\lt[/latex] V when the smallest element of [latex]U\triangle V[/latex] lies in U.

- Take U = S (the full set). For any V [latex]\ne[/latex] S, [latex]S\triangle V=S-V[/latex], whose minimum is in S. So S is smaller than every other subset [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S2 true.
- Take V = [latex]\emptyset[/latex]. For any U, [latex]U\triangle\emptyset=U[/latex], minimum in U, so U [latex]\lt\emptyset[/latex]. So [latex]\emptyset[/latex] is larger than every other subset [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S1 true.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true

options: Both S1 and S2 are true
S1 is true and S2 is false
S2 is true and S1 is false
Neither S1 nor S2 is true
